# Cyber Threats Lurk in Kids' Gaming: What Parents Should Know

### Understand potential risks to help young gamers safely explore exciting worlds online

![A teen boy plays a video game at a laptop in the dark. ](/themes/custom/common_sense/components/commonkit/atoms/ck-image/images/ratio_16_9_large.png)

Video games have long been popular with teenagers, but gaming has become an increasingly dominant part of childhood, with younger kids now gaming more than ever. While gaming offers many benefits, it also comes with genuine risks; understanding these risks can help families set appropriate boundaries and keep kids safe while still enjoying what games have to offer.

The latest [Common Sense Census: Media Use by Kids Zero to Eight](/sites/default/files/research/report/2025-common-sense-census-web-2.pdf) shows that gaming time has increased by 65% since 2020, with children age 8 and under now playing for an average of 38 minutes per day. And it makes sense: Video games have many real benefits for kids, like helping [support creativity](https://www.nyu.edu/about/news-publications/news/2024/may/video-games-can-have-a-positive-impact-on-children---if-designed.html#:~:text=New%20research%20finds%20that%20digital%20games%20can,must%20design%20games%20to%20support%20positive%20outcomes.&text=The%20three%20studies%20found%20that%20games%20can,help%20them%20regulate%20emotions%20and%20build%20relationships) and even [boost cognitive performance](https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/video-gaming-may-be-associated-better-cognitive-performance-children). But as parents and educators navigate this evolving digital landscape, it's important to understand the real risks found in "sandbox" games—open-world games where players can freely explore, create, and interact with others, like Fortnite, Roblox, and Minecraft. Awareness of these risks helps keep both children and the whole family safe, whether they're online or offline.

Like real playgrounds, online games need rules and oversight to protect kids and keep them safe. Modern gaming accounts often collect valuable personal information, saved payment methods, and digital items worth real money. This makes them attractive targets for cybercriminals, leading to financial loss, identity theft, and danger for young gamers.

### **Go Phishing**

Gaming platforms have created their own economies using virtual currencies like V-Bucks (Fortnite), Robux (Roblox), and Minecoins (Minecraft). While these might seem like play money to kids, they have actual cash value and attract sophisticated criminals. In one instance, a user lost [over $2 million worth](https://securelist.com/game-related-threat-report-2023/110960/) of in-app purchases after their account was hacked. While this is an extreme example, even unexpectedly losing $50 can be tough, and victims aren't likely to recoup much of their losses, if any.

When hackers launch *phishing* attacks—which are deceptive attempts to steal personal information by pretending to be trustworthy sources—their goal is to trick players into clicking dangerous links or downloading harmful attachments. **Kids are often targeted with fake links promising free in-game rewards, rare items, or cheat codes** that instead lead to websites that steal account information.For example, scammers create fake sites or apps that claim to offer free or heavily discounted V-Bucks, Robux, or other gaming currencies. When players enter their account details, scammers steal their login credentials.

Once hackers gain access to an account, they typically follow a [common pattern](https://www.allstateidentityprotection.com/business/content-hub/cybercriminals-use-fortnite-to-target-children-bank-accounts) to profit from this theft. They usually start by making unauthorized purchases with any payment methods saved to the account, often buying expensive items or large amounts of in-game currency. These stolen virtual items are quickly transferred to other accounts under their control, making them harder to recover. The criminals then convert these stolen goods into real money by selling virtual items or entire compromised accounts on third-party marketplaces. Finally, they may use the hacked account to send messages to a player's friend list, attempting to spread their scams to more players.

**Think your kids' account may have gotten hacked?** [Read our tips](/articles/what-can-i-do-if-my-kids-device-or-account-has-been-hacked) on what to do next.

### **Dangerous Downloads**

[Recent investigations](https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/internet-security/scam-alert-fake-minecraft-roblox-hacks-on-youtube-hide-malware-target-kids/) have shown that cybercriminals use platforms like YouTube or GitHub to spread *malware*—software designed to damage or steal data from computers—disguised as "game mods" (modifications that change or enhance games). These malicious programs are designed to steal passwords, payment information, and personal data, often targeting more than just gaming accounts. Kids and teens are particularly vulnerable to this because they often lack experience in identifying online scams. The promise of features like "Aimbots" (to improve shooting accuracy) or "Anti-Ban" systems (to avoid getting caught by game administrators) makes these fake downloads even more tempting. Scammers exploit kids' curiosity and eagerness, as they're more likely than adults to take risks without thinking, to trick them into downloading harmful software onto personal or family devices.

![](/sites/default/files/featured-content/avaritia-modfor-minecraft.jpg)

**Since children often use their parents' credit cards for in-game purchases, cybercriminals target them to obtain payment details or personal data that can be exploited to** [**commit fraud**](https://www.experian.com/blogs/insights/online-gaming-fraud/) **or can be** [**sold on the** ***dark web***](https://www.securitymagazine.com/articles/93226-stolen-fortnite-accounts-reportedly-earn-hackers-millions-per-year)**.** The connected nature of today's gaming creates additional security risks. Many players reuse passwords across multiple platforms, or link their gaming accounts to social media, which means a single breach can potentially give hackers access to multiple accounts. In 2023, hackers used a type of malware called [SpyNote](https://securelist.com/game-related-threat-report-2023/110960/) to target Roblox players by disguising it as a game mod. Once installed, this malware could secretly track everything typed on the keyboard, record the screen, and access the device's camera. It could even mimic official Google and Facebook apps to deceive users into revealing their passwords.

### **When Online Dangers Go Offline**

One of the most serious risks in online gaming goes beyond in-game scams or hacked accounts—it's the possibility of [children interacting with predators](https://ussafe.org/children-and-online-predators/) who use these platforms to target young users. Online multiplayer games allow kids to chat with friends *and* strangers. And while most of these players may be harmless, some have far more dangerous intentions.

![](/sites/default/files/featured-content/chatfeature.jpg)

**Predators build trust by connecting with kids through games, and then move kids to less moderated apps. This tactic, known as** ***grooming*****, is designed to isolate young users from trusted adults.** In some cases, this escalates to [sextortion](https://www.fbi.gov/contact-us/field-offices/nashville/news/sextortion-a-growing-threat-targeting-minors), where predators pressure kids into sharing personal information or explicit images by using threats and manipulation, and then demand payment to keep from sharing this content with others. These risks aren't just [hypothetical](https://www.bloomberg.com/features/2024-roblox-pedophile-problem/)—the anonymity of gaming platforms makes it easier for predators to blend in. And because these conversations often happen outside of parental supervision, kids may not recognize red flags until they're already in a dangerous situation that can lead to [tragic outcomes](https://www.usatoday.com/story/life/health-wellness/2025/02/25/teenage-boys-mental-health-suicide-sextortion-scams/78258882007/).

While these risks are real and important to recognize, they shouldn't prevent kids and families from enjoying gaming and online interactions altogether. Knowledge truly is power, and education is your best defense against potential dangers. By staying informed, setting boundaries, and communicating openly, families can confidently navigate digital spaces—ensuring that the fun continues without compromising safety.

### **How Kids and Parents Can Stay Safe**

**For Kids: Protect Your Gaming Experience**

* **Never share login details**: If someone claiming to be from a game company asks for your password, it's almost certainly a scam. Even if the request looks legit, real developers have alternative verification methods that don't involve you sharing your password.
* **Avoid "too good to be true" deals**: Free currency generators and hacks are almost always scams. When in doubt, [take nine seconds to think](https://pausetake9.org/) before clicking.
* **Stick to official stores and downloads**: Only download games, mods, and software from official websites or app stores.
* **Report suspicious behavior**: If someone asks for personal information or tries to lure you to an outside website, report them through the game's official moderation tools ([Roblox](https://en.help.roblox.com/hc/en-us/articles/203312410-How-to-Report-Rule-Violations), [Fortnite](https://safety.epicgames.com/en-US/policies/reporting-misconduct), [Minecraft](https://help.minecraft.net/hc/en-us/request/new?ticket_form_id=4416074743565)) and tell a trusted adult.
* **Enable two-factor authentication (2FA)**: [Many gaming platforms](https://2fa.directory/us/#gaming) offer this extra layer of security—like requiring a code from a cellphone—to prevent unauthorized access.

**For Parents: Keep Your Child's Gaming Safe**

* **Use parental controls:** [Many platforms offer settings](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/positively-media/202311/how-and-why-to-use-parental-controls-in-video-games) to limit in-game purchases, prevent interactions with strangers, and even filter out inappropriate language in chat.
* **Monitor purchases and account activity:** Keep an eye on in-game transactions to prevent unauthorized spending.
* **Build digital literacy:** Help your child think critically about what they see. Discuss why some content is inappropriate, and how to spot warning signs.
* **Review games together:** Check the games your child has recently played and talk about any content that doesn't seem age-appropriate. Our [family tech planners](/family-tech-planners) can help inspire conversations about what kinds of games, devices, and sites are appropriate.
* **Encourage open communication:** Let your kid know they can talk with you about anything uncomfortable that they experience. (It may help to reassure them that you won't stop them from playing altogether.)
* **Teach kids to spot red flags:** Explain to your child that if someone asks to chat on another app or platform, or if they request personal details, these are red flags. Helping your child understand why we don't share personal information like full names, school details, or phone numbers can keep everyone safe.
* **Take control of your family's digital security:** [Get step-by-step guidance and personalized recommendations](https://securityplanner.consumerreports.org/) from our friends at Consumer Reports to secure your online accounts, devices, and personal information, helping you reduce cyber risks and strengthen your digital safety.

**Ready to dive deeper?** Check out our Parents' Ultimate Guides on [Roblox](/articles/parents-ultimate-guide-to-roblox), [Fortnite](/articles/parents-ultimate-guide-to-fortnite), and [Minecraft](/articles/parents-ultimate-guide-to-minecraft) to learn more about these popular online games.

**Share your story**. If your family has had an experience involving hacking, phishing, or other cyber crimes that you are comfortable sharing with us, please fill out [this form](https://forms.gle/iM5Wn4kUR3XgiBkq8) or send us a note at [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#1972707d6a787a6d707677597a76747476776a7c776a7c37766b7e). These stories help us in our work to make the internet and online gaming safer and healthier for all kids.

## What is Fortnite?

If your kids say they're playing Fortnite, they're probably talking about [Battle Royale](/app-reviews/fortnite-battle-royale), the free-to-play multiplayer offshoot of the action-strategy game Fortnite from developer Epic Games. This ultra-popular video game blends elements of sandbox building games with fast-paced action. It offers two modes: a solo version called Save the World and the multiplayer version called Battle Royale. (Note: If you're looking for more parental insights on your kids' favorite things online, sign up for our [family movie night newsletter](/newsletters).)

## What is Fortnite: Battle Royale?

The game allows up to 100 people to participate in a match together. Players are dropped onto the game map and must compete to be the last one standing by killing every other player. During the game, players collect weapons, build safe structures, and try to avoid the Storm that damages all players outside of a safe zone. Players can also choose to play a no-build version, where you just focus on shooting people. Unlike the Save the World version, there aren't any zombies to kill, which makes it a less scary version to play. However, players can buy items to make themselves look like a zombie or another creepy character.

## Do you play by yourself or with a team in Fortnite: Battle Royale?

There are four modes of play in Battle Royale: Solo, Duo, Trio, and Team. In Solo mode, you're dropped into the game alone. In Duo, you're dropped in with one teammate, and in Trio, with two. In Team mode, you play on a team of four. Duos, Trios, and Teams can either be friends choosing to play together or randomly matched players. All players in a match are playing in the same mode.

## What if I'm not ready for the action of Battle Royale?

Don't worry if you've never played Fortnite or a battle royale game before. Playground mode lets players get used to the mechanics of the game without the pressure of fighting other gamers. Playground sessions are limited to a maximum of four players, and you can even put everyone on the same team to eliminate the possibility of friendly fire.

## What is Save the World?

Save the World is the traditional solo campaign in the game Fortnite. Unlike in Battle Royale, where players compete against each other, players in the Save the World mode are survivors of an apocalyptic storm where the few remaining humans must band together to defeat creepy zombie-like creatures called husks.

## Why is my kid so interested in playing Fortnite?

Kids love Fortnite for lots of reasons. One is that it combines two other genres that are big winners with young gamers. Another is that it has a more cartoonish look than some other more gory video games, so younger gamers are drawn to it.

Kids can play with friends in Duos, Trios, and Teams, creating a more social element. And popular gamers like play the game on streaming sites like YouTube and Twitch. Plus, in the case of the Battle Royale mode, it's free (although it does have in-app purchases—more on that below).

## Is Fortnite appropriate for kids? What age should kids be to play Fortnite?

For some parents, the cartoonish, bloodless style of the action in Fortnite makes the violence less problematic than the aggressive gore in other popular shooter games. But the game's online chat feature—especially in Battle Royale mode—could expose younger players to offensive language or mature content from random strangers. Common Sense recommends Fortnite for teens 13 and up, primarily because of the action violence. But with the [right controls](https://privacy.commonsense.org/evaluation/Fortnite) and parental guidance, this can be a preteen-friendly alternative to violent first-person shooters.

## Are there parental controls for Fortnite?

Yes, adults can restrict some features on their child's account. You can manage permissions for friend requests, voice and text chat, content ratings, and filters for mature language. Parents and caregivers can also set up passwords for in-game spending. When you enable this option, the Parental Control PIN will be required for all purchases. Accounts for users under 18 also have privacy settings turned on by default. [Use this guide](https://safety.epicgames.com/en-US/parental-controls) to set up parental controls on your child's account.

There is an additional restriction for kids under 13. Children below that age are automatically assigned a "[cabined account](https://www.epicgames.com/site/en-US/cabinedaccounts)," where parents and caregivers have to consent to their child getting access to certain features. These include in-game purchases and chatting. Keep in mind that the game determines a user's age based on the date of birth they enter when setting up an account.

## Is Fortnite too violent for kids?

Fortnite: Battle Royale is loaded with violence, but it's all cartoonish, rather than bloody or gory. Since the object is to be the last one standing, you'll constantly shoot other players and dodge fatal storms. However, there's no blood; defeated enemies simply vanish.

Those seeking a less violent—and more social—play experience can find it in the weapon-free Party Royale section, which you choose when you log in for a session. Party Royale has no killing and dying. Instead, the environment is more conducive to exploring environments while chit-chatting with friends and other players.

## How much does Fortnite cost?

Players can currently download and play Fortnite: Battle Royale for free. The current cost of Fortnite: Save the Worldis $39.99, although the developer, Epic Games, has suggested it will make it free or discounted some time in the future.

However, even within the free-to-play version, players can spend real money. Fortnite encourages purchases such as upgrades to Deluxe and Super Deluxe editions, as well as in-game currency called V-Bucks that can be used to buy bonus items.

The Premium Battle Pass requires a $10 subscription that lets players compete on more levels and win exclusive game skins/costumes. Epic's partnerships with popular entities including [Marvel](/articles/marvel-age-by-age-guide), [the Mandalorian](/tv-reviews/the-mandalorian), [Predator](/movie-reviews/predator), and [Tron](/search/tron) mean they frequently introduce new characters, costumes, and other crave-worthy elements—keeping players' interest up and their money coming in.

## What are Fortnite Seasons?

Unlike other multiplayer games, Battle Royale has a storyline, which results in frequent additions of new content to the game that are referred to as a new "season." Seasons seem to update approximately every 10–12 weeks, and 10 seasons make up a chapter. You'll begin to see clues to the updates during the current season, usually to encourage players to purchase the next season's Battle Pass.

## What are Fortnite Live Events?

The platform's live events, which are often tied to a feature in the game, can attract tens of millions of viewers (not just players) around the world. Some of the most popular events include concerts, such as ones by Marshmello, Travis Scott, and Diplo, as well as in-game promotional launches, such as director J.J. Abrams' release of an exclusive *Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker* trailer in advance of the movie.

Some of these events are scheduled and some are spontaneous. If your kid's into Fortnite, they'll probably hear the buzz and want to tune in. Events tend to be family-friendly and are listed in the [news section of the Fortnite site](https://www.epicgames.com/fortnite/en-US/news).

## What platforms can you play Fortnite on?

You can play Fortnite on the latest game consoles (PlayStation, Xbox, and Switch), computers (Mac and Windows), and [Android mobile devices](/app-reviews/fortnite-battle-royale). The one place you can't play it is on iPhones, since Epic Games [launched a very public battle against the Apple App Store](https://www.cnet.com/news/apples-battle-with-epic-games-could-lead-to-big-changes-in-iphone-apps/) over the way Apple collects in-app purchase fees—money Epic relies on, as it offers Fortnite: Battle Royale for free.

Users need an internet connection to play. Players can play "cross-platform," which means, for example, that a Windows player can be on a team with a console player. Gamers can also create an account on any device and carry over their progress in a game to another system. For example, you could start on a cellphone, then pick up a game on a computer or console later in the day and continue where you left off.

## How is Fortnite related to Twitch?

Some kids aren't only playing Fortnite—they're watching other people, including celebrities like Drake, play the game on Twitch. Twitch is a social media platform for gamers where they can livestream themselves playing popular video games, including Fortnite. Livestreaming can be unpredictable, so make sure to check out which gamers kids are watching, and if kids say they want to livestream themselves, carefully consider the risks.

## Can players chat with each other in Fortnite: Battle Royale?

Live, unmoderated chat is possible between users in the console and PC versions of Fortnite: Battle Royale. Options include voice chat and on-screen text chat. This exposes players to random strangers and the likelihood of profanity.

## How do you turn off voice chat in Fortnite: Battle Royale?

Open the Settings menu in the top right of the main Fortnite page by selecting the three bars, then the cog icon. Choose the Audio tab at the top of the screen. From there, you can adjust several audio features, including voice chat. Turn the setting from on to off by tapping the arrows.

## How long is a match of Fortnite: Battle Royale?

Each match in Battle Royale lasts about 20 minutes, although players who are killed early play for less time.

## How do I manage screen time for my kids when they're playing Fortnite?

When each match only takes 20 minutes, it's easy to fall into the trap of "just one more" ... sort of like how you end up binge-watching an entire season of [*Stranger Things*](/tv-reviews/stranger-things). But you can take advantage of the quick matches by using them as a natural stopping point in gameplay. Some kids benefit from using a timer, limiting themselves to a certain number of matches per day, or using one of [these tips for finding a balance between gaming and other activities](/articles/how-can-i-help-my-kids-develop-good-screen-time-habits).
